title: The Hearing
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 29 of 40
content:
The Wizengamot chamber was built to make one person feel small.

Rows of benches rose in a dark semicircle. Wizards and witches in plum-colored robes looked down toward a single chair in the center. Torches burned blue-white along stone walls. Every whisper multiplied under the high ceiling.

Snape sat alone.

I sat behind the witness rail with McGonagall, Professor Flitwick, Madam Pomfrey, and three people from the Ministry evidence office.

Harry Potter sat two rows ahead.

He looked older than the photographs from the war and younger than the burden attached to his name.

When Snape entered, Harry stood.

Snape noticed.

His face gave nothing away.

The hearing began.

Kingsley Shacklebolt presided, not as sole judge but as Minister and chair of the review panel. His voice was calm.

“Severus Snape, this proceeding concerns your legal status following the fall of Tom Riddle, your acknowledged membership in the Death Eaters, your subsequent service as an informant and operative, your conduct as Headmaster of Hogwarts, and complaints regarding your conduct as a teacher.”

Snape's mouth tightened at the final clause.

Good, I thought.

All of it.

The first questions were factual.

When did he join?

Shortly after leaving Hogwarts.

Did he accept the Dark Mark voluntarily?

Yes.

Did he pass information to Voldemort concerning a prophecy?

Yes.

Did he understand whom it would endanger?

Not initially.

When he discovered Lily Potter was a target, did he ask Voldemort to spare her?

Yes.

Did he ask for James Potter or Harry Potter to be spared at that time?

No.

The chamber shifted.

Snape did not.

His answers were clipped, exact, merciless toward himself.

Then came the turn.

Did he approach Dumbledore?

Yes.

Did he thereafter provide intelligence against Voldemort?

Yes.

For how long?

Years.

Did he protect Harry Potter?

A pause.

“Yes.”

Harry looked down.

The evidence followed.

Mission logs.

Letters.

Dumbledore's stored instructions.

Our potion analyses showing deliberate sabotage of coercive draughts.

The hidden Carrow cache.

Detention rosters altered during Snape's year as Headmaster.

Statements from students.

Some grateful.

Some furious.

One described how Snape had redirected a punishment that might have left permanent injury.

Another described being humiliated in Potions until they abandoned a planned career.

Snape listened to both with the same still face.

When asked about the second, he said, “The complaint is accurate.”

A panel member blinked.

“You do not contest it?”

“No.”

“Do you believe your conduct was justified by maintaining discipline?”

“No.”

“House rivalry?”

“No.”

“Then why did you behave that way?”

Snape's jaw tightened.

“Because I was angry, biased, and cruel.”

The chamber went very quiet.

I watched his hands.

Steady.

Only the right thumb moved against his palm.

A self-soothing motion so small no reporter would ever notice.

I did.

Harry testified after lunch.

He walked to the witness chair and looked directly at Snape.

The room seemed to hold its breath.

Harry did not call him a hero.

For that alone, I could have hugged him.

He described facts.

Counter-jinxing a broom during his first year.

Teaching him Expelliarmus indirectly through the dueling club.

Occlumency lessons that were damaging as well as necessary.

Protection.

Hostility.

Dumbledore's plan.

The doe Patronus.

The sword of Gryffindor.

Snape's memories at the end.

Then Harry said, “He hated my father. Sometimes he punished me for it. That was wrong. He also saved my life more than once. That is true too.”

My throat tightened.

Both.

Snape's eyes closed for half a second.

Harry continued.

“I don't think what he did for us means the things he did to students don't matter. And I don't think the things he did wrong mean we get to pretend he didn't help defeat Voldemort.”

Kingsley watched him carefully.

“What are you asking this panel to do, Mr. Potter?”

“Tell the truth.”

Snape looked at him then.

Something passed between them.

Too private for me to interpret.

Good.

The last witness called was me.

I had not expected it.

My stomach dropped when my name was spoken.

Snape's head snapped toward the rail.

I stood.

The walk to the chair felt longer than any corridor at Hogwarts.

I sat.

The panel asked about the audit.

I described the six sabotaged phials.

The hidden Carrow cache.

The altered records.

Snape's attempt to burn the list of names.

His face tightened.

I told that truth too.

“And what prevented destruction of the records?” a witch asked.

“I did.”

“Did Mr. Snape cooperate after that?”

“Yes.”

“Voluntarily?”

“After an argument.”

A few people smiled.

Snape did not.

“What is your professional assessment of him?”

Dangerous question.

I looked at the panel.

“As a potioneer?”

“As a person you have worked closely with.”

The room seemed to narrow.

Snape looked at me.

I remembered every version I refused.

Monster.

Martyr.

Broken man.

Secret saint.

“I don't think that's a professional question,” I said.

Murmurs.

The witch frowned. “You may still answer.”

“No. I can tell you what I observed. He is an exceptional potioneer. He is exacting. He is difficult. He attempted to protect people whose names appeared in compromised records. He accepted corrections to those records when challenged. He has acknowledged harmful conduct toward students without asking me to excuse it. He has repeatedly provided evidence against his own interest when accuracy required it.”

I paused.

“He is not simple enough for a character assessment to be useful evidence.”

Snape's face changed.

Just slightly.

The witch leaned back.

“Do you trust him?”

That question was personal.

I could have objected.

I looked at Snape.

“Yes,” I said.

His breath caught.

“With what?” she asked.

“Laboratory safety. Evidence. My boundaries. Information that could damage him.”

Another pause.

“My no.”

The chamber went quiet.

Snape looked down.

The questioning ended soon after.

The panel withdrew.

We waited for nearly two hours.

No one spoke much.

Harry sat on one side of the corridor.

Snape sat on the other.

At one point Harry stood, crossed the space, and offered Snape a cup of water.

Snape took it.

“Thank you,” he said.

Harry nodded.

That was all.

It felt like enough.

When the doors reopened, everyone returned.

Kingsley read the decision.

Snape would not be prosecuted for actions taken while acting as Dumbledore's operative or for Dumbledore's death, which the evidence established had been carried out under prior agreement.

His earlier Death Eater service was formally acknowledged in the record.

His later cooperation and wartime service were also formally acknowledged.

No prison sentence.

No loss of wand rights.

A civil review of former-student complaints would remain available.

His professional teaching status would be left to Hogwarts and the Board of Governors.

No declaration of heroism.

No erasure.

Legal status.

Public record.

Consequences.

Exactly what I had told him the Ministry could provide.

Snape stood.

For a moment he looked as though he had no idea what to do with being allowed to leave.

Then Kingsley said, “Mr. Snape.”

He looked back.

“Thank you for your testimony.”

Snape's mouth tightened.

“I would prefer never to repeat it.”

Kingsley almost smiled.

“A reasonable preference.”

Outside the chamber, reporters waited upstairs.

Snape looked at me.

“After,” he said.

I stepped closer.

“After.”

This time, before the lift doors opened, his hand found mine.
